title: Reinterpreting the Pavlik Concept Through Rehabilitation Engineering: From Dynamic Stability to a Controlled Movement Environment—A Perspective on Movement as a Research Variable
content: Rehabilitation interventions do not act independently of the physical conditions in which movement occurs. Orthoses, positioning systems, and movement-assistance devices modify the mechanical conditions under which movement is performed. The Pavlik harness provides a classical clinical example. Developed for the treatment of developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH), it maintains the hip in a therapeutic position while allowing a degree of movement within mechanically imposed constraints [1–3]. The Pavlik method was developed within pediatric orthopedics rather than rehabilitation engineering. Its clinical logic can nevertheless be reconsidered from an engineering perspective: movement may be guided by modifying its mechanical environment rather than simply eliminating movement. Modern rehabilitation technologies provide ways to make selected movement conditions explicit, adjustable, and reproducible. Continuous passive motion (CPM) is one such example, because joint movement can be generated according to predefined mechanical parameters [4]. This Perspective does not propose CPM as an extension or replacement of the Pavlik method. The relationship is conceptual rather than therapeutic. Pavlik illustrates mechanical guidance with preserved movement; CPM illustrates how a movement condition can be translated into a programmable mechanical input. The central proposition is therefore narrower: the physical conditions surrounding movement can themselves become variables for rehabilitation engineering research.
